━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🏦 UNDERSTANDING ECB POLICY DECISIONS

The European Central Bank drives EUR price action through interest rates and bond purchases. Unlike the Fed, the ECB manages policy for 20 different economies, making decisions more complex.

Key tools traders watch:

- Main refinancing rate - sets borrowing costs across eurozone
- Deposit facility rate - what banks earn on ECB deposits
- Asset purchase programs - quantitative easing or tightening

Real example: When ECB raised rates by 50bps in July 2022, EUR/USD rallied 300 pips in two days. Markets had priced in only 25bps, creating the surprise move.

How to trade ECB events:

- Watch pre-meeting leaked reports from Reuters or Bloomberg
- Compare ECB dot plot forecasts versus market pricing
- Listen for hawkish or dovish language in Lagarde press conferences
- Track eurozone inflation data two weeks before meetings

PRO TIP: ECB typically moves slower than the Fed. When rate differentials widen between USD and EUR, it creates multi-month trends. Trade the differential, not single meetings.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🧠 BEATING FOMO IN YOUR TRADING

Fear Of Missing Out destroys more accounts than bad strategy. You see a pair rocket 200 pips and jump in at the top. We have all done it.

Why FOMO happens:

- Social media showing winning trades creates pressure
- Watching price move without you triggers emotional response
- Recency bias makes you remember missed opportunities more than saved losses

Classic FOMO scenario: Bitcoin pumps 15 percent in four hours. You enter at resistance. Price dumps 8 percent next two hours. You panic sell at a loss. Then it continues up without you.

Breaking the FOMO cycle:

- Keep a trade journal noting every FOMO entry and its result
- Set alerts at your entry levels, then close the charts
- Remember that markets create new opportunities every single day
- Ask yourself: Would I take this trade on my strategy if price was flat?

If the answer is no, stay out.

SMART MONEY RULE: Professional traders miss moves constantly. They do not chase. They wait for the next setup with proper risk-reward. There is always another trade.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💡 THREE WEEKEND TRADING TIPS

Tip 1 - Review Your Week Before Monday Open

Take 30 minutes Sunday evening. Check your trading journal. Calculate your win rate. Identify your best and worst trades. What pattern do you see? Most traders repeat the same mistakes weekly until they actively review.

Tip 2 - Mark Key Levels on Higher Timeframes

Weekend is perfect for clean chart analysis. Mark weekly and daily support-resistance levels. These hold more weight than intraday levels. When markets open Monday, you will have a roadmap instead of reacting randomly.

Tip 3 - Check the Economic Calendar for the Week

Know which days have high-impact news. ECB meetings, NFP, CPI, GDP releases. Plan your trading around these events. Either trade the breakout or stay flat. Never hold risky positions through major data unaware.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

⚠️ POSITION SIZING: THE 1 PERCENT RULE

Most beginners focus on entry and exit. Professionals obsess over position size. This determines whether you survive long enough to become profitable.

The 1 percent rule: Never risk more than 1 percent of your account on a single trade.

Account size 10,000 USD. Maximum risk per trade equals 100 USD. You set stop loss at 50 pips. Your position size calculates to 0.20 lots on EUR/USD.

Why this matters:

- Ten losing trades in a row only draws down 10 percent
- You stay emotionally stable through losing streaks
- You can trade your strategy with discipline, not fear

Common mistake: Risking 5 percent per trade means 5 losses drops you 25 percent. Now you need 33 percent gain just to break even. The math works against you.

Adjust for volatility: On high-impact news days or volatile pairs like GBP/JPY, consider dropping to 0.5 percent risk. Protect your capital first.

SMART MONEY RULE: You cannot control if a trade wins or loses. You can control how much you lose. Position sizing is the only true control you have in trading.
